vignette:
David still feels the cold metal of the handcuffs around his wrists, even though the bruises faded months ago. He is sixty-one years old, a bus driver for thirty years, married to Linda for thirty-five, and he cannot remember the faces of the men who tortured him. He remembers the smell of diesel and sweat, the strip of duct tape across his mouth, the jolt of electricity that made his teeth clench so hard he thought they would crack. But the moments in between-the long stretch when they dragged him to the back of the bus, the bargaining in a language he did not understand-those are gone, as though a film editor had cut out every frame that did not show pain. He remembers the terror, though. It comes back whole. Whenever he hears a key turn in the front lock after dark, his chest seizes and his palms sting with sweat, and for a split second he is back on the floor of his own bus, waiting for the next shock. That terror does not dull with time; it only waits.

The hijacking happened eighteen months ago, on his regular morning route through the industrial part of town. Two men boarded at a stop near the scrap yard, and within minutes they had pulled guns and ordered everyone to the floor. They made David drive forty minutes into the countryside, then forced him into the luggage bay and took the passengers one by one to the front seats. He could hear crying, but he could not see. Then they came for him. They wanted him to call a dispatcher and say the bus had broken down, to buy them more time. He did it. He did everything they said. That is the part he cannot forgive himself for-not fighting, not signaling, not doing something. He is certain now that he is a weak person, that a real man would have found a way to protect the people on his bus. The passengers were eventually released, unharmed, but David tells himself that was luck, not his doing. He should have protected them. He failed.

In the weeks afterward, David went back to work because he did not know what else to do. He drove the same routes, but he stopped looking at passengers directly. Every reflection in the rearview mirror made him flinch. A dropped backpack sent his heart hammering against his ribs, and he would pull over, breathless, while his hands shook on the wheel. His supervisor noticed and suggested a desk assignment, but David refused-he thought if he gave in, he would be admitting that the men had broken him. So he kept driving, but he avoided the industrial stretch by taking a longer detour through residential streets, adding thirty minutes to his schedule. The passengers complained. He got written up. Linda asked him why he was coming home so late, and he told her he was just tired. He did not tell her that every night he checked the locks on the doors and windows three times, then lay awake listening for footsteps in the hallway, convinced that someone was about to enter their home. He did not tell her that when she got up to use the bathroom, the sound of the door opening made him gasp and grab the bedside lamp as a weapon.

The guilt has settled into a fixed belief: he does not deserve to feel safe. He replays the moment when he handed over the radio and said the bus was broken down, and he thinks I should have said something else, I should have risked it. The gaps in his memory torment him more than the clear parts, because he imagines that the missing pieces hold evidence of his cowardice-things he did that he has now blocked out. He has come to believe that the real story is worse than what he can recall.

What finally brought David to the clinic was his wife's ultimatum. Six weeks ago, she found him at two in the morning standing in the kitchen doorway, a knife in his hand, staring at the back door because he thought he heard someone trying the lock. There was no one there. She cried and said she could not live like this anymore, that he was not the man she married. He agreed to see someone because he could not bear the thought of losing her, but inside he is certain that no talking will change what he did. He walks into the therapist's office with his shoulders hunched, expecting to be told that he is right-that he is weak, that he failed, that the terror is his punishment. But part of him, the part that still wakes up shaking, hopes that someone might show him how to stop listening for footsteps that never come.
